o7.setup: You run a small options book. On Thursday you sold the Nifty 24,000 straddle expiring next Tuesday: the 24,000 call and the 24,000 put, for 420 points in all. The Union Budget comes out on Monday.
facts: Short the 24,000 call and the 24,000 put

steps.text: Before the Budget, your risk manager asks what kind of risk the book is running.
steps.ask: Which describes your position?

options.text: Short gamma and short vega: big moves and rising volatility both hurt
options.why: Selling options leaves you short both. Theta, the daily decay, is what you're paid for taking that risk.

options.text: Long gamma and short vega: big moves help, rising volatility hurts
options.why: Owning options gives long gamma. You sold them, so your gamma is short.

options.text: Short gamma and long vega: big moves hurt, rising volatility helps
options.why: Higher implied volatility makes options dearer, and you're short them, so rising volatility hurts: you're short vega.

steps.text: By Friday the Nifty is still at 24,050, but implied volatility on your expiry has jumped from 13% to 18% as traders buy protection before the Budget. Your book shows a loss.
steps.ask: Why are you losing money when the Nifty hasn't moved?

options.text: Higher implied volatility has made the options you sold dearer
options.why: You're short vega, so a rise in IV marks your short options up and shows as a loss, even with no move in the Nifty.

options.text: Theta works against option sellers
options.why: Theta is on your side: the options you sold lose value each day, all else equal.

options.text: The straddle has picked up a lot of delta
options.why: With the Nifty still near your strike, the straddle is close to delta neutral. Delta isn't the cause.

steps.text: Budget day. The Nifty falls 2% to about 23,570, so the 24,000 put you sold is now well in the money.
steps.ask: What's your delta now?

options.text: Long: you lose more if the Nifty keeps falling
options.why: A short put has positive delta, and it grows as the put goes into the money, while the short call's negative delta fades. Net, you're long the market.

options.text: Short: you lose more if the Nifty bounces
options.why: That would be true after a rally, when the short call dominates.

options.text: Zero: a straddle is always delta neutral
options.why: It's only near neutral at the strike. Moves away from the strike build delta; that's what gamma means.

steps.text: The fall could run further this afternoon, and your risk limits say to cut the directional exposure now.
steps.ask: What's the most direct way to do that?

options.text: Sell Nifty futures sized to your delta
options.why: Futures carry delta but no gamma or vega, so selling them flattens the market exposure the fall has built up. That's delta hedging.

options.text: Sell more puts to collect extra premium
options.why: More short puts add long delta and short gamma, which doubles the risk you're meant to cut.

options.text: Do nothing: theta will earn it back by expiry
options.why: A few days of decay is small next to a 2% move. Counting on theta to cover a gamma loss is how short-option books blow up.

steps.text: Tuesday morning, with the Budget behind it, the Nifty steadies near 23,700 and implied volatility drops from 18% back to 12%.
steps.ask: What does the drop in IV do to your book?

options.text: Helps: the options you're short lose value
options.why: This is IV crush. Being short vega, you gain as implied volatility falls after the event.

options.text: Hurts: lower IV means less premium on new trades
options.why: That matters for your next trade, not this one. Your existing short options just got cheaper, which is a gain.

options.text: Nothing: IV only matters on expiry day
options.why: IV feeds into option prices every day until expiry. By expiry day, only intrinsic value is left.

steps.text: Expiry day arrives. The Nifty has drifted back to 23,990, right next to your 24,000 strike, with a few hours to go.
steps.ask: What's the main risk now?

options.text: Gamma is at its highest: small moves flip your delta, so hedges go stale fast
options.why: Hours from expiry, an at-the-money option's delta can swing from near 0 to near 1 on a small move. That's pin risk, and why many desks close short strikes before the last hour.

options.text: Vega is at its highest, so any change in IV hurts
options.why: Vega shrinks as expiry nears. With hours left, gamma is the Greek that matters.

options.text: Theta stops working on expiry day
options.why: At-the-money options decay fastest on expiry day. The danger is gamma, not a lack of theta.

steps.text: You buy back the whole straddle for 30 points in all and close the futures hedge.
steps.ask: Before costs and the hedge, what did the straddle make per unit?

options.text: 390 points
options.why: Sold for 420, bought back for 30: 420 − 30 = 390 per unit.

options.text: 420 points
options.why: That's the premium you collected. Buying back cost 30 of it.

options.text: 450 points
options.why: Buying back is a cost, so subtract the 30 rather than add it.

x4.setup: A fund wants to buy 4 lakh shares of a large-cap stock today. The portfolio manager decided to buy at 9:20, with the stock at ₹1,000, but the order only reaches your desk at 10:00, with the stock at ₹1,004. The PM will judge you against the day's VWAP.
facts: Normal daily volume: about 40 lakh shares

steps.ask: The stock rose from ₹1,000 to ₹1,004 before the order reached you. What's that ₹4 called?

options.text: Delay cost
options.why: It's the move between the PM's decision and the order arriving, 40 bp here. It counts in implementation shortfall even though nobody has traded yet.

options.text: Market impact
options.why: Impact is the move your own trading causes, and you haven't traded yet.

options.text: Spread cost
options.why: Spread cost comes from crossing the bid-ask spread when you trade.

steps.text: Before choosing an algo, you size the order up.
steps.ask: What share of a normal day's volume is this order?

options.why: 4 lakh ÷ 40 lakh = 10%. Big enough to move the price if rushed, small enough to spread over the day.
4 lakh is a tenth of 40 lakh, not a hundredth.
That mixes up the order size with the daily volume.

steps.ask: With the PM measuring you against the day's VWAP, which approach fits best?

options.text: A VWAP algo running to the close
options.why: It trades in step with the stock's usual volume pattern, which is exactly what the benchmark measures.

options.text: One market order now for all 4 lakh shares
options.why: Sending it all at once would sweep the order book and pay heavy impact.

options.text: A TWAP algo that finishes by noon
options.why: Equal slices over two hours ignore the volume pattern and cram a tenth of the day's volume into a short window, a far higher participation rate.

steps.text: The algo spreads the order over the rest of the day in line with volume. By noon, about 30% of the volume left in the day has usually traded.
steps.ask: If the algo is on schedule, roughly how many shares has it bought by noon?

options.text: About 1.2 lakh
options.why: Following the volume profile, it should have done 30% of 4 lakh, which is 1.2 lakh.

options.text: About 2 lakh
options.why: That's half the order, but only about 30% of the remaining volume has traded.

options.text: About 30,000
options.why: That's 30% of 1 lakh. The order is 4 lakh.

steps.text: At 1 pm a headline says a rival fund is buying the same stock, and the price jumps 1%. The PM still wants all 4 lakh shares today.
steps.ask: What should you do with the rest of the order?

options.text: Raise the urgency and finish sooner, accepting more impact
options.why: The price is running away. Waiting now carries more timing risk than the extra impact of trading faster, and the PM needs the full size.

options.text: Pause until the price comes back down
options.why: It may not come back. If it keeps rising, the shares you haven't bought turn into opportunity cost.

options.text: Keep exactly the same schedule
options.why: The schedule ignores the news. With another buyer in the stock, sticking to it leaves you buying at ever higher prices later in the day.

steps.text: A colleague notices your algo is buying exactly 5,000 shares every 30 seconds.
steps.ask: Why is that a problem?

options.text: Other traders can spot the pattern and buy ahead of you
options.why: Regular, same-sized child orders leak information. Traders who spot them buy first and sell to you higher.

options.text: Exchanges don't allow repeated orders of the same size
options.why: There's no such rule. The issue is what the pattern gives away.

options.text: It breaks the participation limit
options.why: The size is fine against the volume. The problem is how predictable the orders are.

steps.text: You finish at 3:20 pm with an average price of ₹1,012.
steps.ask: What's the implementation shortfall against the decision price, before fees?

options.text: 120 bp
options.why: (1,012 − 1,000) ÷ 1,000 = 1.2%, which is 120 bp. It includes the 40 bp of delay before you got the order.

options.text: 80 bp
options.why: That's against the arrival price of ₹1,004. Shortfall is measured from the decision price.

options.text: 12 bp
options.why: ₹12 on ₹1,000 is 1.2%, which is 120 bp, not 12.

steps.text: Twenty minutes after you finish, the stock has slipped back to ₹1,006.
steps.ask: What does that suggest?

options.text: Part of the rise was your own temporary impact, so the end was probably rushed
options.why: When the price falls back once you stop buying, some of what you paid was temporary impact. That's post-trade reversion.

options.text: Sellers have lost interest in the stock
options.why: A fall right after a big buyer stops points to the buying having pushed the price up, not to sellers leaving.

options.text: Nothing: prices always wander after an order
options.why: Some noise is normal, but a steady fall right after a big buyer stops is a known sign of temporary impact.

f3.setup: You run an arbitrage book. A large-cap stock trades at ₹2,000 in the cash market, and its near-month future, 30 days from expiry, trades at ₹2,016. You can borrow and lend at 6.5% a year, and no dividend is due before expiry.

steps.ask: What's the future's fair value?

options.why: That's where the future trades, not where it should trade.

options.text: About ₹2,130
options.why: That charges a full year of interest instead of 30 days.

steps.ask: The future is about ₹5 over fair value. Which trade captures that?

options.text: Buy the stock and sell the future
options.why: That's cash-and-carry arbitrage: it locks in the ₹16 basis, more than the ₹10.7 it costs to fund the stock.

options.text: Sell the stock and buy the future
options.why: That's the reverse trade, for when the future is cheap. Here it's rich.

options.text: Buy the future on its own
options.why: That's a bet on the stock rising, not an arbitrage.

steps.ask: Roughly what annualised return does the ₹16 basis lock in, before costs?

options.text: About 9.7% a year
0.8% a year
options.why: 0.8% is what you earn in 30 days. Scale it up to a year.

options.text: About 16% a year
options.why: 16 is the basis in rupees, not a percentage.

steps.text: Your round-trip costs (brokerage, STT, exchange charges and the rest) come to 0.25% of the position.
steps.ask: Is the trade still worth doing?

options.text: Only just: about 6.7% a year after costs, against 6.5% to borrow
options.why: 0.8% − 0.25% = 0.55% in 30 days, about 6.7% a year. It barely beats the cost of funding the stock.

options.text: Yes, easily: costs hardly matter in an arbitrage
options.why: On a thin, locked-in spread, costs are most of the story.

options.text: No: the costs are bigger than the basis
options.why: 0.25% is less than the 0.8% basis. The trade clears its costs, just not by much.

steps.text: You do the trade. A week later the stock has fallen 5% to ₹1,900 and the future to ₹1,913.
steps.ask: What's happened to your P&L per share?

options.text: Up about ₹3
options.why: The stock lost 100 and the short future gained 103 (2,016 − 1,913). The basis narrowed from 16 to 13, and that's your gain so far.

options.text: Down ₹100
options.why: That ignores the short future, which gained as the stock fell.
That counts the future's gain but forgets the stock's 100 loss.

steps.text: On expiry day the stock closes at ₹2,050.
steps.ask: Before costs, what has the whole trade made per share?

options.why: The future settles at the closing price of 2,050. The stock gained 50 and the short future lost 34 (2,050 − 2,016): 50 − 34 = 16, the basis you locked in.
That's only the stock leg. The short future lost 34.
That's only the futures leg. The stock gained 50.

steps.text: You'd like to keep the trade going. Next month's future trades at ₹2,051 with the stock at ₹2,050 and 35 days to go.
steps.ask: Should you put the same trade on in next month's future?

options.text: No: at ₹2,051 the future is below its fair value of about ₹2,062.8
options.why: Carry for 35 days is about 2,050 × 6.5% × 35/365 ≈ 12.8. A future only ₹1 over spot is cheap, so buying stock and selling it would earn less than the funding cost. If anything, it suits the reverse trade for someone who owns the stock.

options.text: Yes: any positive basis is free money
options.why: The basis has to beat the cost of funding the stock, about ₹12.8 here, plus trading costs.

options.text: Yes: futures always converge to spot, so it can't lose
options.why: Convergence locks in the basis, but ₹1 is far less than the ₹12.8 it costs to fund the stock for 35 days.

y4.setup: It's Wednesday. The Nifty is at 24,000 after a sharp fall last week, and options expiring next Tuesday look expensive. You expect the Nifty to stay between 23,500 and 24,500 until expiry. Your rule: never hold a position whose loss isn't capped.
facts: Implied volatility: high after last week's fall
Your rule: every loss must be capped

steps.ask: Which structure fits your view and your rule?

options.text: Sell an iron condor: the 23,500–23,300 put spread and the 24,500–24,700 call spread
options.why: It earns premium if the Nifty stays in your range, and the bought wings cap the loss on both sides, as your rule needs.

options.text: Sell the 23,500 put and the 24,500 call, a strangle
options.why: It fits the range view, but nothing caps the loss on a big move, so it breaks your rule.

options.text: Buy the 24,000 straddle
options.why: A long straddle needs a big move, the opposite of your view, and it buys options while they're expensive.

options.text: Buy the 24,000–24,500 call spread
options.why: That's a bet on a rally. Your view is a range.

steps.text: You sell the condor for a net credit of 70: 35 for the put spread and 35 for the call spread. Each spread is 200 points wide.
steps.ask: What's your maximum loss per unit, and when?

options.text: 130, if the Nifty ends below 23,300 or above 24,700
options.why: Only one side can lose at expiry. That side's 200-point width minus the 70 credit for the whole condor leaves 130.

options.text: 330, if the Nifty ends outside both wings
options.why: The Nifty can't end below 23,300 and above 24,700 at once, so only one spread can lose.

options.text: 200, the width of one spread
options.why: The credit you took in counts against the loss: 200 − 70 = 130.

options.text: 70, the credit collected
options.why: 70 is your maximum profit, kept if the Nifty ends between 23,500 and 24,500.

steps.text: Friday: the Nifty rallies to 24,420, close to your short 24,500 call. The call spread is now worth 110 and the put spread 5, so the condor costs 115 to close: a loss of 45. Your risk manager says this trade must not lose more than 100 a unit.
steps.ask: What do you do?

options.text: Close the whole condor for 115, locking in a loss of 45
options.why: At 115 the loss is 45, inside the limit, and nothing is left to go wrong. Holding on risks 130 if the rally runs past 24,700.

options.text: Buy back only the call spread and keep the put spread
options.why: That takes off the rally risk, but the put spread is then a trade of its own that could lose up to 165, with no call side to offset it. Closing both locks the loss at 45 with no risk left.

options.text: Hold: the wings already cap the loss
options.why: They cap it at 130, which is past the 100 limit.

options.text: Sell another 24,500–24,700 call spread to bring in more credit
options.why: That adds to the side that's losing. Another rally would double the damage.

steps.text: Tuesday, expiry day. At 10 a.m. the Nifty is at 24,000, and a colleague suggests selling a fresh condor expiring today, the 23,800–23,700 put spread and the 24,200–24,300 call spread, for a credit of 12.
steps.ask: What's the main risk in that trade?

options.text: Gamma: a 1.25% move today can take it to its full loss of 88
options.why: On expiry day near-the-money options swing hard with the Nifty. A rise to 24,300 is only 1.25%, and the call spread would lose its full 100 minus the 12 collected.

options.text: Vega: a jump in implied volatility
options.why: With hours left there is almost no time value, so vega barely matters. The swings come from gamma.

options.text: Theta: the options decay against you
options.why: Theta works for a seller. It's the one thing on your side today.

options.text: Delivery of shares if the options end in the money
options.why: Nifty options are cash-settled, so nothing is delivered.

steps.text: Back to your condor: it lost 45 a unit, against a worst case of 130.
steps.ask: What kept the loss small?

options.text: Capping the risk from the start and acting on the loss limit early
options.why: The wings set a worst case before the trade began, and closing early kept the loss well inside it.

options.text: High implied volatility, which guaranteed a profit
options.why: High IV pays more premium but guarantees nothing. The rally nearly broke the call side.

options.text: Iron condors win most of the time, so the size didn't matter
options.why: A high probability of profit with a lopsided payoff makes size the main risk, not a detail.

y6.setup: You manage a ₹10 crore portfolio of large Indian stocks with a beta of 1.2 to the Nifty. The Union Budget is next week, and the investment committee wants protection against a market fall without selling any stocks.
facts: Lot size: 65, so one lot is about ₹16.25 lakh
Goal: protection for about two weeks

steps.ask: Which trade gives the protection?

options.text: Sell Nifty futures against the portfolio
options.why: Short futures gain as the market falls, offsetting the stocks, and you keep every share.

options.text: Buy Nifty futures
options.why: Long futures lose in a fall too. They add to your exposure instead of offsetting it.

options.text: Buy Nifty calls
options.why: Calls pay when the market rises. They don't protect a portfolio of stocks you own.

options.text: Sell the stocks and buy them back after the Budget
options.why: That's what the committee wants to avoid: it costs spreads, impact and tax, and you may miss a rebound.

steps.ask: How many lots do you sell to take out the market risk?

options.text: About 74 lots
options.why: Beta × portfolio ÷ one lot: 1.2 × ₹10 crore ÷ ₹16.25 lakh ≈ 73.8, so about 74 lots.

options.text: About 62 lots
options.why: ₹10 crore ÷ ₹16.25 lakh ≈ 61.5 ignores beta. A portfolio with beta 1.2 tends to move 20% more than the Nifty.

options.text: About 51 lots
options.why: That divides by the beta instead of multiplying: ₹10 crore ÷ 1.2 ÷ ₹16.25 lakh ≈ 51.

steps.text: You sell 74 lots. On Budget day the Nifty falls 3%, but your stocks fall 4%, because the banks you hold had a bad day of their own. The stocks lose ₹40 lakh and the futures make about ₹36 lakh.
steps.ask: Why isn't the hedge perfect?

options.text: A beta hedge only covers the market part of the move; the extra fall came from your stocks themselves
options.why: A beta hedge removes market risk. What's left is the stocks' own moves, here the banks' bad day, and that stays with you.

options.text: You sold too few lots
options.why: 74 lots matched the beta. The gap came from stock-specific moves, which no index hedge removes.

options.text: Futures don't follow the Nifty on Budget day
options.why: Futures track the index closely. The basis can shift a little, but that isn't the main gap here.

steps.text: A week later the market has steadied, and the committee wants half the protection off.
steps.ask: What do you do?

options.text: Buy back about 37 lots
options.why: Buying back half the short futures halves the hedge, and the stocks stay untouched.

options.text: Sell 37 more lots
options.why: That adds to the short futures, doubling the protection instead of halving it.

options.text: Sell half the stocks
options.why: That cuts the exposure too, but the committee wants to keep the stocks. The futures are the tool for changing it.

steps.text: The futures you're short expire next Tuesday, but the committee wants the remaining hedge kept for another month.
steps.ask: How do you keep the hedge on?

options.text: Roll it: buy back this month's futures and sell next month's before expiry
options.why: Rolling carries the hedge into the next month. You pay the gap between the two months, the roll cost.

options.text: Do nothing: the hedge carries on by itself
options.why: Index futures are cash-settled at expiry, and then the position is gone.

options.text: Sell next month's futures and keep this month's as well
options.why: Until this month's expire you'd hold twice the hedge, an over-hedge that bets on a fall.

z4.setup: You trade a pair of two large private banks, A and B. Over five years the spread between them has swung around its average, with a half-life of about eight trading days. Your rules: enter when the spread's z-score passes ±2, exit near 0, and stop out at ±4 or after 40 trading days.
facts: Pair: Bank A against Bank B, equal rupee amounts
Enter at a z-score of ±2, exit near 0
Stop at ±4 or after 40 trading days

steps.text: Today the z-score is +2.3: Bank A is unusually dear against Bank B, and neither has news.
steps.ask: What's the trade?

options.text: Sell Bank A and buy Bank B in equal rupee amounts
options.why: A positive z-score means A is dear against B, so you sell the dear one and buy the cheap one, betting the gap narrows.

options.text: Buy Bank A and sell Bank B
options.why: That bets the gap widens further, the opposite of the snap-back your rules trade.

options.text: Sell both banks
options.why: That's a bet on the sector falling, not on the gap between them.

options.text: Wait for +4 to get a better entry
options.why: +4 is your stop. Waiting for it means trading only when the pair may be breaking.

steps.text: You can't keep an ordinary short in cash shares overnight unless you've borrowed them, and both banks have stock futures.
steps.ask: How do you hold the short side for days?

options.text: Sell Bank A futures, matched as closely as the lot size allows to the rupee value of the Bank B leg
options.why: Stock futures let you stay short for days. Matching rupee amounts makes the market's moves mostly cancel.

options.text: Short Bank A shares in the cash market and hold them
options.why: A cash short without borrowed shares has to be bought back the same day.

options.text: Buy a put on Bank B
options.why: That's a bet against the wrong stock: Bank A is the dear one.

steps.text: About three weeks later the z-score is back to 0.2.
steps.ask: What now?

options.text: Close both legs: the gap is back near its average
options.why: Your rule exits near 0. The edge was the stretch, and with it gone, staying in is just holding two banks against each other.

options.text: Hold until the z-score reaches −2
options.why: That's a new bet that the gap overshoots the other way. Your rules don't trade it.

options.text: Add to the trade
options.why: There's no stretch left to bet on.

steps.text: A month later you're in a new trade on the same pair, short A and long B at +2.1. Then Bank B announces it will take over a large lender, paying with new shares. B falls 8% and the z-score jumps to +4.4.
steps.ask: What do you do?

options.text: Stop out: the deal changes what Bank B is, so the old relationship may no longer hold
options.why: This is what the stop is for. A big change in one company can break the tie between the two, and a broken pair can keep moving against you.

options.text: Double the position: the gap has never been this wide
options.why: It's wide because something real changed. Adding to a broken pair is how stat arb books blow up.

options.text: Hold and wait the usual eight days
options.why: The half-life was measured on the old relationship. After the deal it may not apply.

steps.ask: Before trading this pair again, which check matters most?

options.text: Re-test the pair for cointegration on prices after the deal, and trade small until it holds
options.why: The old statistics describe the old bank. Fresh data has to show the gap still comes back.

options.text: Check that daily returns are still highly correlated
options.why: Daily moves can stay highly correlated while the prices drift apart. Cointegration is the test that matters.

options.text: Widen the stop to ±6 so it isn't hit again
options.why: That keeps you in broken pairs for longer. The stop did its job.

z5.setup: You've built a trend-following system on Indian index and currency futures. In the backtest it made 14% a year with a Sharpe ratio of 1.1. Before it trades real money, the risk committee wants answers.
facts: Markets: Nifty, Bank Nifty and USD/INR futures
Rule: long above the 100-day average, short below it

steps.text: The backtest assumed every trade filled at the closing price, with no costs.
steps.ask: What should you add first?

options.text: Realistic costs: brokerage, STT, exchange fees, slippage and the cost of rolling futures each month
options.why: Costs come out of every trade. With about 40 trades a year and a roll in each market every month, they can take a big bite out of 14%.

options.text: More markets, to raise the return
options.why: Maybe later. First find out what the current system earns after costs.

options.text: A shorter average, so it trades more often
options.why: More trades means more costs, which the backtest hasn't counted yet.

steps.text: After costs it makes 10% a year. You tried 30 different average lengths, and 100 days did best.
steps.ask: What's the main worry?

options.text: The 100-day choice may be overfitted: picked because it did best on this data
options.why: Taking the best of 30 versions on the same data flatters the result. Check nearby lengths, and data the choice never saw.

options.text: 100 days is too long to count as a trend
options.why: Trend systems often use 50 to 200 days. The length isn't the issue; how it was picked is.

options.text: 10% a year is too little to bother with
options.why: That's a judgment for later. First check whether the 10% is real.

steps.text: Every length from 60 to 150 days makes between 8% and 10% after costs, and the years you kept aside give 9%.
steps.ask: What does that tell you?

options.text: The edge doesn't hang on one setting, so it's more likely to be real
options.why: A broad plateau of similar results, plus a matching test on unseen years, is what a sturdy signal looks like.

options.text: The system will make 9% a year from now on
options.why: Nothing guarantees future returns. Trends come and go, and a change in how markets behave can stall a system for years.

options.text: Switch to 60 days, since shorter is better
options.why: Picking again by backtest repeats the overfitting problem, and shorter lengths trade more, so they cost more.

steps.text: The committee asks how big the fund can grow.
steps.ask: What limits it?

options.text: Capacity: past some size, your own trades move the futures enough to eat the edge
options.why: Index futures are deep, so slow trend systems can run large sums, but every strategy has a size past which impact costs win.

options.text: Nothing: futures markets are deep enough for any size
options.why: Even deep markets charge for size. Impact grows with the size of each order.

options.text: The number of trades a year
options.why: Trading less often helps, but the limit is the market impact of each trade.

steps.text: Live, the system loses money for seven months in a row while markets go sideways.
steps.ask: What's the sound response?

options.text: Check it's within what the backtest showed for flat markets, and keep risk at the planned level
options.why: Trend systems have long flat stretches. If this drawdown fits the backtest's range, quitting now locks in the losses just before the next trend.

options.text: Switch it off: seven losing months prove it's broken
options.why: Not on their own. Compare them with the backtest's worst stretches before deciding.

options.text: Double the size to win it back faster
options.why: Raising risk after losses to recover them is how drawdowns turn into disasters.
